lesson.title: Keep the rows that answer the question

lead.text: Say the owner's rule to the table: units of 3 or more. In pandas it is written df['units'] >= 3. The comparison does not pick anything out yet. It is made against every row separately, and the answer for each row is either True or False. For the four orders, with 2, 1, 3 and 4 units, the answers are False, False, True and True.

That column of True and False values is called a mask. It has one entry for each row of the table, in the same order, so the mask and the table line up. Think of a stencil laid over the table: the holes are the True entries, and only the rows showing through the holes are kept. A value exactly at the limit passes a >= test, which is why the order of 3 units is True.

Laying the stencil over the table is written df[mask]. It keeps the rows where the mask is True and leaves out the rest. Each kept row comes through whole, with its shop, units and price still together, so the data on a row never gets separated from the row itself.
Step through the two cases. Both build a mask first and then use it. The first tests units. The second tests the shop name with ==, which asks whether two values are equal.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the mask reads False, False, True, True, so rows 2 and 3 survive and keep their original row numbers. In the second case the shop is Bay in rows 0 and 2, so those two come through. A single equals sign stores a value and two equals signs ask a question, so a test for equality always uses ==. The mask can be stored under a name, as it is here. It can also be written straight inside the brackets.

    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],

})
mask = df['units'] >= 3
result = df[mask]

lead.text: The test is made on each value separately. A value equal to the limit passes a >= test.

Often one rule is not enough. The owner may want only Bay's orders of 3 units or more. That needs two masks, one for the shop and one for the units, joined so that a row is kept only when both are True. The joiner for “and” is & and the joiner for “or” is |. Each comparison goes in its own brackets, and the whole expression goes inside df[...]: df[(df['shop'] == 'Bay') & (df['units'] >= 3)].

The word and will not do here. It wants a single yes or no for the whole column, and a column of True and False values has no single answer, so pandas stops with an error. The symbols & and | work on each row separately. They also bind more tightly than a comparison does, which is why every comparison needs its own brackets.
The figure joins the same two masks with & in the first case and with | in the second.

afterFigure.text: With &, only the third order passes, since it is the only one that is both from Bay and of 3 units or more. With |, a row passes when at least one test is True, so both Bay orders come through along with Hill's order of 4 units.

lead.text: A mask asks a yes-or-no question of each row. A new column can hold a number worked out from each row instead. Arithmetic between two columns happens row by row, just as array arithmetic happened position by position. df['units'] * df['price'] multiplies the units of each order by that order's own price. Storing the result under a name the table does not have yet, as in df['revenue'] = df['units'] * df['price'], adds a new column.

An assignment does not have to come from another column. df['fee'] = 4 puts the single value 4 into every row of a new column, repeated to fit the table, so the column's total is 4 times the number of rows. Step through the figure, where the first case adds revenue and the second removes a column.

afterFigure.text: The first case adds a revenue column holding 10, 8, 15 and 32, one figure for each order. The second case uses drop, which returns a copy of the table without the named column and leaves df itself as it was. The revenue for the whole shop is then the sum of the new column.

lead.text: Multiply each order's units by its own price before you add anything up.

The last job is a price correction. The owner finds that Bay's price should be 6, and the change is wanted in the Bay rows only. loc, which you used with labels in the last lesson, accepts a mask for the rows. df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] reads the prices of the Bay rows. Adding .sum() would total them. Put an equals sign after it and it writes to those cells instead: df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] = 6.

It is tempting to do the job in two steps, selecting the Bay rows first and assigning afterwards, as in df[df['shop'] == 'Bay']['price'] = 6. That is chained indexing. The first step hands back a separate table, and the assignment goes to that table, so df does not change. Older versions of pandas sometimes let it through, which is why it still turns up in old code. A single loc call names the rows and the column together and writes straight to df.
Step through the figure. The first case corrects the Bay prices and the second the Hill prices.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the two Bay rows now hold 6 and the Hill rows keep 8. In the second case only the Hill rows change, to 9. The mask picks the rows, the second value picks the column, and the number after the equals sign is written into those cells only. Rows the mask leaves out are never touched.

blocks.text: A small online shop has four orders on its list. Bay ordered 2 units, Hill ordered 1, Bay ordered 3 and Hill ordered 4. The shop ships an order free when it holds 3 units or more, and the owner wants to see which orders qualify.

On four rows she can check by eye. On four thousand she needs the table to do it, and she needs to state the rule once and have it applied to every row. The same table then has to answer follow-up jobs, such as the takings from each order, or a price entered wrongly for one shop that must be corrected in that shop's rows alone.
This lesson works through those jobs on the four orders. It begins with testing each row against a rule and ends with changing a column in exactly the rows that pass.

intro.promise: By the end you'll filter a table with a mask, combine two conditions, and add or change a column on exactly the rows you mean.

recap.keyIdea: A comparison gives a mask with a True or False for each row, & and | join masks when each comparison is in brackets, column arithmetic works row by row, and one loc call changes exactly the rows you chose.

blocks.text: You found that only one row passes both a shop test and a units test when they are joined with &. You worked out revenue of 33 from three orders, and the price column totals 34 after the Bay correction.

recap.nextHook: Every table so far had a value in every cell. Real tables have gaps: a customer skips a question, or a sensor loses a reading. The next lesson shows how pandas marks a gap, and what a total or an average does when it meets one.
